title: Week 1 · Lesson 1: Cellular Injury & Adaptation — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 1 — Lesson 1: Cellular Injury & Adaptation

FNP-level goal: Use cellular mechanisms to explain presentation, identify threats to tissue viability, build a focused differential, and recognize when outpatient evaluation is unsafe.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish adaptation, reversible injury, irreversible injury, necrosis, and apoptosis.
  • Explain ATP depletion, ion-pump failure, calcium overload, oxidative stress, and reperfusion injury.
  • Connect cellular injury to symptoms, biomarkers, inflammation, and organ dysfunction.
  • Recognize red flags that need emergency evaluation.

Part 1 — The Clinical Framework

When a cell is stressed, ask: Is it reversible? Is perfusion/oxygen delivery threatened? Has injury become irreversible?

Normal cell → adaptation → reversible injury → irreversible injury → cell death.

Severity and duration of the insult, cell type, metabolic demand, and collateral blood supply influence the outcome. The same exposure can affect two patients very differently.

Part 2 — Adaptation Is a Clinical Clue

Adaptation may preserve function initially, but persistent stress can become maladaptive.

  • Hypertrophy: increased cell size; chronic hypertension can cause left-ventricular hypertrophy.
  • Hyperplasia: increased cell number in tissues able to divide; unopposed estrogen can cause endometrial hyperplasia.
  • Atrophy: decreased cell size and often function; immobilization can cause skeletal-muscle atrophy.
  • Metaplasia: replacement by a mature cell type better able to tolerate stress; Barrett esophagus is a clinical example.

FNP connection: adaptation should prompt a search for the chronic driver, not treatment of the structural response in isolation.

Part 3 — Ischemia, Hypoxemia, and Hypoperfusion

Hypoxemia is low arterial oxygen; ischemia is inadequate tissue blood flow. Ischemia is especially damaging because it reduces oxygen and substrate delivery while limiting metabolite removal.

Common mechanisms include coronary thrombosis, acute limb ischemia, stroke, shock, severe anemia, sepsis-related microcirculatory dysfunction, and compartment syndrome.

Reduced perfusion/oxygen delivery → impaired oxidative phosphorylation → ATP falls.

Part 4 — ATP Failure: The Core Cascade

ATP supports membrane pumps, protein synthesis, volume regulation, and repair.

ATP ↓ → Na+/K+-ATPase failure → intracellular Na+ ↑ → water enters → cellular swelling.

ATP depletion also impairs calcium handling:

Ca2+ accumulates in cytosol and mitochondria → phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases, and ATPases activate → membrane, protein, cytoskeletal, and DNA injury.

Early injury may be reversible if perfusion is restored before critical membrane and mitochondrial injury. Persistent injury can cross the threshold to cell death.

Part 5 — Mitochondria and Irreversible Injury

Mitochondria are the major source of ATP and a major target of injury. Severe calcium overload and oxidative stress disrupt mitochondrial membrane integrity and oxidative phosphorylation. Once the cell cannot restore energy balance and membrane integrity, injury is irreversible.

This is why time-sensitive reperfusion matters in myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and acute limb ischemia.

Part 6 — Reactive Oxygen Species and Reperfusion

Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are normal signaling products in controlled amounts. Excess ROS causes oxidative stress.

  • Lipid peroxidation damages cell and organelle membranes.
  • Protein oxidation impairs enzymes and structural proteins.
  • DNA damage can activate repair pathways, apoptosis, or mutation.

Antioxidant defenses include superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione. Reperfusion is essential to salvage tissue, yet it can also generate ROS and contribute to calcium overload, endothelial dysfunction, and sterile inflammation.

Ischemia → ATP depletion. Reperfusion → oxygen returns, but ROS and inflammatory injury may transiently intensify tissue damage.

Part 7 — Reversible vs Irreversible Injury

Reversible injury may include cellular swelling, reduced ATP production, fatty change in selected organs, and temporary loss of function.

Irreversible injury is characterized by profound mitochondrial dysfunction and major membrane injury. Do not wait for permanent injury to become obvious before escalating when a history suggests threatened perfusion.

Part 8 — Necrosis vs Apoptosis

Necrosis

Necrosis commonly follows severe injury, especially sustained ischemia. Cells swell, membranes lose integrity, intracellular contents leak, and inflammation follows.

Necrosis → membrane disruption → intracellular contents enter blood/tissue → inflammation.

Clinical links: cardiomyocyte injury can raise troponin; hepatocellular injury can raise aminotransferases; skeletal-muscle injury can raise creatine kinase. Biomarkers must be interpreted with timing, symptoms, examination, ECG/imaging, and the full differential.

Apoptosis

Apoptosis is regulated cell death. Cells shrink, nuclear material fragments, apoptotic bodies form, and phagocytes clear them with relatively little surrounding inflammation. It is important in normal development, tissue turnover, and removal of cells with irreparable DNA damage.

Part 9 — Tissue Pattern Matters

  • Heart: chest pressure, dyspnea, diaphoresis, arrhythmia, reduced contractility.
  • Brain: sudden focal deficit, speech difficulty, visual change, altered mental status.
  • Kidney: rising creatinine, oliguria, electrolyte and acid-base abnormalities.
  • Gut: severe pain, sometimes pain out of proportion to early examination, metabolic derangement.
  • Limb: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia.

The cellular cascade is shared; presentation, time sensitivity, and differential depend on the organ.

Part 10 — FNP Clinical Reasoning: Acute Chest Symptoms

Pressure-like chest discomfort, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, syncope, or an anginal equivalent may represent myocardial ischemia: acute coronary-flow reduction → ATP depletion → reversible ischemia or irreversible cardiomyocyte injury.

Do not anchor on one diagnosis. Time-sensitive differentials include acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, aortic syndromes, tension pneumothorax, severe arrhythmia, and esophageal rupture when supported by the presentation.

Focused assessment includes onset, exertional relationship, quality, radiation, associated symptoms, risk factors, vital signs, perfusion, cardiopulmonary examination, and urgent ECG/emergency assessment when indicated.

Part 11 — Initial Management and Disposition

The FNP role is to recognize possible tissue-threatening disease, stabilize within setting and scope, activate emergency pathways, and give a concise mechanism-based handoff.

Emergency evaluation: ongoing/recurrent concerning chest pain, new focal neurologic deficit, acute limb-ischemia signs, severe dyspnea or hypoxemia, hypotension/shock, syncope with instability, altered mental status, or suspected sepsis with poor perfusion.

Handoff: presentation + onset + vital signs/perfusion + key findings + highest-risk differential + actions taken.

Part 12 — Board-Style Case 1

A 63-year-old patient has crushing substernal pressure, diaphoresis, and nausea. ECG and serial biomarkers are obtained urgently.

Mechanism: acute coronary-flow reduction → myocardial ischemia → ATP depletion → pump failure and calcium overload → possible irreversible injury and necrosis.

FNP decision: recognize possible acute coronary syndrome and arrange emergency evaluation; do not wait for a definitive clinic diagnosis.

Part 13 — Board-Style Case 2

A patient with atrial fibrillation abruptly develops severe leg pain, pallor, paresthesia, and absent distal pulse.

Think: embolic arterial occlusion → acute limb ischemia → threatened ATP-dependent tissue function. Neurologic deficit or threatened-limb findings are an emergency.

FNP High-Yield Framework

Stress → adaptation or injury

Ischemia → oxygen/substrate delivery ↓ + waste removal ↓ → ATP ↓

ATP ↓ → ion-pump failure → swelling + Ca2+ overload → mitochondrial/membrane injury

Persistent injury → irreversible injury → necrosis/apoptosis and organ dysfunction

FNP decision: identify the threatened organ, consider dangerous alternatives, obtain appropriate urgent evaluation, and do not delay escalation when perfusion may be at risk.
